text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNState the assumptions of diffusive shock acceleration, obtain the relativistic-particle energy slope from compression, and distinguish acceleration time from maximum energy. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01A shock can do more than heat gas Shock jump conditions constrain the bulk gas, but particles that repeatedly cross the front can form a high-energy population far from thermal equilibrium. Consider a steady, planar, nonrelativistic shock and particles with speed v ≈ c. In the shock frame let w₁ > w₂ > 0, with compression χ = w₁/w₂. Scattering by magnetic irregularities approximately isotropizes particles in each local fluid frame. Use the test-particle limit, in which accelerated particles do not modify the flow. A static magnetic field does no work on a charge. Energy comes from the bulk flow as particles scatter between moving frames. Significant motion of scattering centres relative to the gas modifies the simple spectral result below. 02Gain and escape in one cycle For a small relative flow speed, changing between fluid frames changes relativistic particle energy by approximately (w₁−w₂)μ/v to first order. Crossing particles are flux-weighted by the direction cosine μ, giving mean μ = (∫₀¹μ²dμ)/(∫₀¹μdμ) = 2/3. Two crossings make a complete cycle. g ≡ ⟨ΔEE⟩cycle ≈ 4(w₁−w₂)3v For downstream particle number density np, the isotropic crossing flux is npv/4. The advective loss flux far downstream is npw₂. Their ratio gives the escape probability per cycle. Pesc ≈ 4w₂v Both are first order in flow speed divided by particle speed. This is the origin of the name first-order Fermi acceleration. This idealization neglects escape through the upstream boundary. 03Eliminate the cycle count to get a power law Start N₀ particles at E₀. After k surviving cycles, Ek = E₀(1+g)k and Nk = N₀(1−Pesc)k. Take logarithms and eliminate k. N(>E)N₀ = (EE₀)ln(1−Pesc)/ln(1+g) N(>E) ∝ E−Pesc/g The second line uses ln(1+g) ≈ g and ln(1−Pesc) ≈ −Pesc for small gains and losses. N(>E) is cumulative. The differential number distribution per energy interval is its negative derivative, adding one to the index. dNdE ∝ E−s, s = 1+Pescg s = 1+3w₂w₁−w₂ = χ+2χ−1 A strong monatomic gas shock has χ = 4, giving s = 2 for relativistic particles per energy interval. A momentum-space distribution function uses dN = 4πp²f(p)dp, so the same solution is written f(p) ∝ p−4. 04A spectral slope does not set the maximum energy Describe scattering by spatial diffusion coefficients κ₁ and κ₂. A residence layer has thickness of order κ/w. Dividing its particle content by crossing flux nv/4 gives tcycle ≈ (4/v)(κ₁/w₁ + κ₂/w₂). Dividing by the gain g gives the local logarithmic acceleration time. tacc(E) ≡ EdE/dt ≈ 3w₁−w₂(κ₁w₁+κ₂w₂) For χ = 4 and κ₁ = κ₂ = κ, tacc = 20κ/w₁². If κ depends on energy, the time from E₀ to E is ∫tacc(E′)dE′/E′, not generally a single value of this local timescale. rL = p|q|B ≲ L ⇒ E ≈ pc ≲ |q|BLc SI units; L is the size of the acceleration region. Confinement, source age, downstream advection, upstream escape, and radiative cooling all matter. The slope derivation does not determine injection efficiency or magnetic turbulence. Propagation also means the cosmic-ray slope measured at Earth need not equal the source slope. After a shock leaves electrons and ions at different temperatures, follow their equilibration in two-temperature plasmas. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For compression χ = 3, what is the index s in dN/dE ∝ E−s? Does confinement alone determine the maximum energy? Show the answer and reasoning s = (χ+2)/(χ−1) = 5/2. Confinement is necessary, but acceleration must also fit within the source age and beat cooling or escape. E−2 is conditional on a strong nonrelativistic shock, a test-particle treatment, relativistic particles, and the stated scattering assumptions.
